## References

1. [EnterpriseOps-Gym: Environments and Evaluations for Stateful Agentic Planning and Tool Use in Enterprise Settings](https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.13594)
2. Code: [ServiceNow/EnterpriseOps-Gym @ 271f2c3](https://github.com/ServiceNow/EnterpriseOps-Gym)

# Notes

## The problem: agents that write to real systems

Most tool-use benchmarks test an agent the way you would test a calculator: call a function, check the answer, move on. Each call stands alone. In an enterprise system, that picture is wrong in three ways. First, every write changes the world the next call sees. If you create a support case, then link a knowledge article to it, the second call depends on the ID the first one produced. Second, the work is long: a real request like "wrap up James Hill's HR case" hides several ordered steps that no one spells out. Third, the work is fenced in by rules. Only managers may reassign cases. A case cannot be closed until all its tasks are inactive. A knowledge article found by automated search must be tagged "suggested", not "applied". Break a rule and you have not just failed a task; you have corrupted a database that other people rely on.

The ServiceNow Research team (with Mila) built EnterpriseOps-Gym to measure exactly this: can an LLM agent plan and carry out long chains of state-changing tool calls while obeying written policy, and can it refuse when the request is impossible or forbidden? Their answer, across 14+ frontier models, is "not yet". The best model, Claude Opus 4.5, completes 37.4% of tasks.

The paper argues that earlier enterprise benchmarks were too shallow to show this. WorkArena and WorkArena++ live inside ServiceNow only; CRMArena and CRMArena-Pro inside Salesforce only; all have fewer than 25 database tables and fewer than 50 tools (Table 1). General tool benchmarks like ToolLLM and ACEBench have thousands of tools but no persistent state at all. [[2406.12045 - Tau-Bench (Tool-Agent-User Interaction)]] and its successor ([[sierra-research-tau2-bench - Agent Evaluation Harness]]) are the closest relatives: they also check the final database state against a goal and also include policy documents. EnterpriseOps-Gym keeps that design and scales the environment up by roughly an order of magnitude: 164 tables and 512 tools versus τ-bench's 3 tables and 28 tools.

## What the environment is, built up from the bottom

**A database per domain.** Each of eight domains (Calendar, Customer Service Management or CSM, Drive, Email, HR, IT Service Management or ITSM, Teams, and a cross-domain Hybrid category) is a relational database whose schema was modelled on public API documentation of real enterprise products, but made vendor-neutral. Across all domains there are 164 tables. The authors measure how tangled the tables are with the average number of foreign keys per table. A foreign key is a column that points at a row in another table, like `case.contact_id` pointing into `contact`. More foreign keys means the agent must look up more related rows before it can build a valid tool argument. The mean is 1.7 per table, from 1.1 in Calendar to 2.4 in HR, which is higher than any prior benchmark in Table 1. A typical task touches a sub-graph of 24.9 tables and about 3,443 rows; Hybrid tasks reach 73 tables.

**Tools on top of the database.** Each domain exposes its operations as tools served over MCP (the Model Context Protocol, a standard way to publish callable functions to an LLM). There are 512 tools in total, from 37 in Calendar to 93 in ITSM. Each domain runs as its own Docker container on its own port. The agent never writes SQL; it calls `find_user`, `create_new_case`, `link_case_knowledge` and so on, and the server translates those into database reads and writes. This is the pattern captured in [[tools-as-database-read-write-for-verifiable-environments]]: if every tool is a read or write against one database, then the whole outcome of an episode is the final database, and grading becomes a query.

**A system prompt that is the policy.** Each task ships with a long system prompt that plays the role of company policy. The CSM example in Appendix B.2 runs to several pages: role definitions (Administrator, Agent, Manager, Customer), a legal state machine for cases ("new → in progress / pending / resolved; ... resolved → closed"), allowed enum values, and rules like "When the knowledge is found through automated search it should be linked as suggested." The agent must read this and apply it without being reminded in the user request. This is what makes the benchmark about planning rather than instruction-following: the user asks for an outcome, and the policy silently adds extra required steps.

**Tasks with a unique end state.** Experts (over 160 contributors hired through Turing, about 20 annotators and 6 reviewers per domain, roughly $100 per task over four months) wrote 1,150 tasks. Each task has a user request, the policy prompt, a starting database snapshot, a human "gold" trajectory, a human natural-language plan, and a set of SQL verification checks. The authors "constrain tasks to have a unique final state, though multiple valid paths may exist to reach it." This is the key design choice. Because the end state is unique, it can be checked with exact SQL. Because the path is not fixed, an agent that finds a different valid order of calls still passes. Expert trajectories average 9.15 steps and reach 34; a task averages 5.3 verification checks and the hardest needs 44.

**Infeasible tasks.** 30 of the 1,150 tasks are designed to be impossible: a needed tool is missing, the request breaks a policy (a scheduling conflict, a data-access rule), or a resource is unavailable (an inactive user, a system "in migration mode"). Each carries about 10 checks, most of which confirm that nothing changed. Passing means refusing cleanly with no side effects. This mirrors the vault idea of [[refusal-tasks-where-inaction-is-optimal]]: some tasks exist only to reward doing nothing.

**Quality filter using the models themselves.** Before human review, draft tasks were run against GPT-5, Gemini and Claude. Trajectories were used to find broken tasks (missing tools, bad data, conflicting access rules) and also to throw out tasks that were too easy. This is worth flagging. It means the benchmark was partly selected against the very model families it later evaluates, which pushes scores down by design. It is a legitimate way to build a hard benchmark, but it means "37.4%" is a statement about a filtered, adversarially-hard distribution, not about the average enterprise request.

## How a run is scored

The agent is a plain ReAct loop: the model reads the conversation, either emits tool calls or stops, tool results are appended, repeat. The main setting is "oracle tools": the agent is only shown the tools the gold trajectory needed (the `selected_tools` list in each task), as if a perfect retriever had picked them. This isolates planning and execution from tool search.

When the agent stops, a list of SQL verifiers runs against the final database. Each is a query plus an expected value, usually `SELECT COUNT(*) ... WHERE <every field that must be right>` with expected value 1. The task score is 1 only if every verifier passes. The paper reports pass@1 averaged over three runs. It also computes a softer "verifier-level" score (the fraction of checks passed) but argues it is misleading, because an agent can pass the easy setup checks and still fail the part that matters.

The verifiers were later sorted by an LLM into three kinds: Task Completion (was the goal reached?), Integrity Constraints (are foreign keys and state consistent?), and Permission and Process Compliance (were policy rules followed?). This split is what lets the paper say where agents fail, not just how often. It is close to the [[four-layer-scoring-stack-for-rl-environments]] idea: separate "did the job" from "did it without breaking things" from "did it by the rules".

## Results, and what is surprising in them

**Headline.** Claude Opus 4.5 averages 37.4%, Gemini-3-Flash 31.9%, GPT-5.2 (High) 31.8%, Claude Sonnet 4.5 30.9%, GPT-5 29.8%. The best open model, DeepSeek-V3.2 (High), gets 24.5%; Qwen3-4B (Think) gets 13.7%.

**Domain matters more than model.** Email, Teams and Drive top out around 51–52%. ITSM tops out at 28.5% and Hybrid at 30.7%. CSM is where open models collapse: Qwen3-235B gets 4.7% there but 38.1% on Email. The pattern is that collaboration tools have few rules and short chains, while CSM, ITSM and HR are policy-heavy with long chains (CSM averages 12.1 steps, Email 6.2).

**Policy is the weakest skill.** Table 7 breaks verifier pass rates by category. Integrity checks pass most often, task completion next, and policy compliance least: 30.0% in ITSM and 45.5% in CSM, versus 81.3% in Teams. In plain words: models usually leave the database consistent and often get the main thing done, but they skip the extra steps the policy requires.

**Longer tasks decay steadily.** Grouping tasks by gold trajectory length, the closed-model mean falls from about 35% at 4 steps to under 20% at 16 steps, and open models fall faster, toward 10%. This is the familiar compounding-error story ([[error-accumulation-in-long-horizon-closed-loop-prediction]], [[no-recovery-bottleneck-in-long-horizon-agents]]): if each step has a small chance of a silent mistake and nothing catches it, success decays roughly geometrically with length.

**Distractor tools do not hurt.** With Sonnet 4.5, adding 5, 10 or 15 extra tools, chosen by Claude to look as relevant as possible, moved scores by +0.07, +2.35 and +0.64 points. So tool selection is not the bottleneck at this scale. A caveat the paper does not dwell on: 15 extra tools on top of about 12 is still a small menu. It says nothing about choosing among all 93 ITSM tools, let alone 512. Compare [[hidden-tools-gate-capability-behind-retrieval]], where retrieval is the gate.

**Plans are the bottleneck, and this is the central finding.** The authors split planning from execution in two ways. In the first, Claude Sonnet 4.5 writes a plan and a weaker model executes it. Kimi-K2, Qwen3-30B and Qwen3-4B gain 5–13 points in CSM, ITSM and HR. In the second, the same weaker models get the human-written plan. Now gains are 14–35 points. Table 3 is striking when you do the arithmetic: Qwen3-4B on CSM goes from 3.8% (ReAct alone) to 37.2% with the human plan. That is higher than Claude Opus 4.5's own unaided CSM score of 34.2%. A 4-billion-parameter model that is given the right plan beats the best frontier model that has to plan for itself.

The authors offer two readings. One: once the plan is external, what remains is following instructions and filling arguments, which even small models do well. Two, more speculative: large models have strong priors and drift from a given plan, while small models follow it literally. The paper does not test the second claim directly.

**More agent architecture does not help much.** For Sonnet 4.5, a planner-then-executor setup adds 10.7 points in CSM and 8.8 in HR. A heavier setup that also splits the task into subtasks, each run by its own sub-agent, does worse: it falls below plain ReAct in CSM (16.2% vs 16.7%). The explanation is that these tasks have strong sequential dependencies. A subtask agent that does not see the IDs and state changes from earlier subtasks cannot fill in later ones. Decomposition assumes the parts are separable, and here they are not. The oracle human plan with the same Sonnet executor sits far above all automated setups (the figure's top bars are in the mid-50s).

**Thinking budget helps, but not everywhere.** For GPT-OSS-120B, going from low to high reasoning effort lifts Drive from 8.6% to 41.0% and Teams from 4.0% to 32.0%. At low effort CSM, ITSM and HR are near zero. But ITSM plateaus at 6.1% from medium to high, and Email peaks at medium. More tokens do not buy knowledge of the policy. This connects to [[agent-test-time-scaling-limited-by-verification-gap]]: extra compute helps only when the model can tell whether it is on the right track.

**Refusal is a coin flip.** On the 30 infeasible tasks the best clean-refusal rate is 53.9% (GPT-5.2 Low), with DeepSeek-V3.2 High at 53.8%. Interesting detail: the low-effort GPT-5.2 refuses better than the high-effort one (50.0%). One plausible reason, not tested in the paper, is that more reasoning makes a model more determined to find a way to complete the request.

**Cost.** Gemini-3-Flash sits on the Pareto front: 31.9% at $0.03 per task, versus Opus 4.5 at 37.4% for $0.36. DeepSeek-V3.2 High gives 24.5% at $0.014.

## What failure looks like up close

Appendix C walks through three Claude rollouts, and they are more useful than any table for seeing what "planning failure" means.

In the ITSM case, two incidents share the number `INC0000004` across two tenants. The lookup tool returns the first match, which belongs to the wrong company, has the wrong status, the wrong description and the wrong assignee. The agent accepts it anyway and links a knowledge article to the wrong incident. It also creates the article with the tool's default `state="published"` even though both the policy and the user's word "draft" require `state="draft"`. The authors' summary: "Both failures share the same pattern: accepting the first plausible result without cross-validating against task context or policy constraints."

In the CSM case (Sonnet 4.6), the agent does nearly everything right: it notices the relevant article is retired and republishes it, creates a missing support group, adds the user to it, links the article. It fails one of five checks because policy says linking an article must move the case to `pending`, and it left that parameter out of its final `update_case` call. One missing field, whole task failed.

In the HR case, "wrap up his case" requires three unstated steps: deactivate both open tasks, set the case to `closed complete`, set the approval status to `approved`. The agent instead turned a task into a survey and then declared success, telling the user that "James can complete the survey as part of the case wrap-up process."

The paper names four recurring patterns: creating records without first looking up prerequisites (dangling foreign keys), missing the follow-up actions a state change triggers, passing IDs that were never resolved through a tool call, and declaring completion too early. All four are planning failures in the sense that the right tool was available and the model knew how to call it.

## How the code implements it

The released repo contains the evaluation harness, three orchestrators, and task configs (the full task set is on HuggingFace; the public split is 60% of tasks). The MCP servers themselves ship only as Docker images, so the tool logic and database schemas are not in the repo.

**1. Each run starts from a clean copy of the world.** State-changing tasks are only comparable if every attempt starts from the same database. Before each run, the executor creates a fresh database on each domain server from the task's SQL seed file and points the client at it.

`benchmark/executor.py:323-349 @ 271f2c3`
```python
            db_id = create_database_from_file(
                gym_conf["mcp_server_url"], gym_conf["seed_database_file"]
            )

            if db_id:
                # Track this database for cleanup
                run_databases.append(
                    {
                        "gym_name": gym_conf["mcp_server_name"],
                        "gym_url": gym_conf["mcp_server_url"],
                        "database_id": db_id,
                    }
                )
                self.auto_created_databases.append(
                    {
                        "gym_name": gym_conf["mcp_server_name"],
                        "gym_url": gym_conf["mcp_server_url"],
                        "database_id": db_id,
                    }
                )

            client = self.mcp_clients.get(gym_conf["mcp_server_name"])
            print(
                f"Created database ID: {db_id} for gym: {gym_conf['mcp_server_name']}"
            )
            if client:
                client.database_id = db_id
```

The server hands back a new database ID, and every later tool call from that client carries it (as an `x-database-id` header, visible in the verifier's SQL call). Many tasks can therefore run in parallel on one container without seeing each other's writes, and the databases are deleted in a `finally` block at the end. For Hybrid tasks the loop runs once per domain, so one episode owns several databases at once. This is the "reset" of the environment in RL terms, and it is what makes the benchmark usable as a training environment too ([[environment-and-eval-are-the-same-object]]).

**2. The agent loop ends when the model stops calling tools.** The benchmark needs a single, neutral agent so that differences come from the model. The ReAct loop is deliberately bare.

`orchestrators/react.py:73-92 @ 271f2c3`
```python
            # Terminate if the LLM decided no further tool calls are needed
            if not response.tool_calls or len(response.tool_calls) == 0:
                logger.info("No tool calls requested. Task complete.")
                break

            # Act + Observe: execute each tool call and feed results back
            for tool_call in response.tool_calls:
                tool_name = tool_call["name"]
                tool_args = tool_call["args"]

                logger.debug(f"Tool arguments: {tool_args}")

                exec_result = await self._execute_tool_call(tool_name, tool_args)
                tool_result = exec_result["result"]
                target_gym = exec_result["gym_server"]

                logger.info(f"Tool result success: {tool_result.get('success')}")

                if tool_name not in tools_used:
                    tools_used.append(tool_name)
```

Termination is entirely the model's choice: a turn with no tool calls ends the episode. That is exactly why "Premature Completion Hallucination" is a failure mode: nothing in the loop checks whether the work is done. Parallel tool calls in one turn are executed one after another, in order, each routed to the right domain server through a tool-to-server map (the Hybrid case). The base class caps the loop at 50 iterations. There is no "refuse" tool; refusing simply means ending without writes, which the infeasible-task verifiers then detect in the database.

**3. A verifier is a SQL count that must equal a number.** The grading must depend only on the final state, not on the path. Here is the verifier list from one CSM task in the repo:

`data/revised/csm/task_20251209_132736_542_99ba2325_6705caf4.json:37-49 @ 271f2c3`
```json
  "verifiers": [
    {
      "verifier_type": "database_state",
      "name": "Verify case creation",
      "description": "Verify case creation",
      "gym_name": "sn-csm-server",
      "validation_config": {
        "query": "SELECT COUNT(*) AS count FROM customer_case WHERE case_id = 1233 AND state = 'in_progress' AND assignment_group_id = 24 AND assigned_to = 427 AND channel = 'email' AND priority = 'critical' AND escalation_reason = 'customer_request' AND escalation = 1;",
        "expected_value": 1,
        "comparison_type": "equals"
      }
    },
```

One query packs eight conditions into a single check: the row must exist with every field right. The user asked to "escalate", and the check demands `escalation_reason = 'customer_request'` and `escalation = 1`; the user asked to recreate a case, and policy says a worked case goes `in_progress`. Notice `case_id = 1233`. The check assumes the new case gets the next auto-increment ID. If an agent creates a stray case first (a wrong attempt it then abandons), the correct case becomes 1234 and this check fails even though the right case exists. So the "unique final state" is stricter than it sounds: it also punishes some harmless extra writes, which acts as an implicit side-effect check.

In the 16 sample tasks shipped in the repo, all 102 verifiers are `database_state` type, and only one expects a count of 0 (an explicit "this must not exist" check). The paper describes verifiers as checking "goal completion, state integrity, policy compliance, and unintended side effects", but in these samples side effects are mostly caught indirectly through fixed IDs like the one above, not through dedicated negative checks. The infeasible tasks, which are not in the local sample, are where negative checks would live.

**4. A hidden second kind of verifier: LLM-as-judge.** The verifier engine supports a type the paper never mentions. For tasks where the answer is text returned to the user rather than a database write, it runs SQL to fetch the truth and asks an LLM to score the agent's final message against it.

`benchmark/verifier.py:138-162 @ 271f2c3`
```python
        sql_query = validation_config.get("sql_query")
        comparison_prompt = validation_config.get("comparison_prompt")
        minimum_comparison_value = validation_config.get("minimum_comparison_value", 7)

        if not sql_query or not comparison_prompt:
            return {"passed": False, "error": "Missing sql_query or comparison_prompt"}

        # Execute SQL query
        sql_result = await self._execute_sql_query(
            sql_query, database_id, context, gym_name
        )

        if not sql_result["success"]:
            return {
                "passed": False,
                "error": f"SQL query failed: {sql_result.get('error')}",
            }

        # Extract LLM response text
        llm_response_text = self._extract_llm_content(model_response)

        # Use LLM as judge
        judge_result = await self._compare_with_llm(
            sql_result, llm_response_text, comparison_prompt, minimum_comparison_value
        )
```

The judge returns a 1–10 score and passes at 7 or more. Note which LLM judges: the verifier is built with the same `llm_client` as the agent under test, so if any task uses this type, a model grades its own answer. The paper's description is SQL-only, and none of the 102 local sample verifiers use this path, so it may be unused in the released benchmark. It is still worth knowing before adding tasks, because a self-judging verifier would quietly weaken the "outcome-based" claim, since the usual LLM-as-judge concerns (self-preference, lenient scoring) would apply.

**5. All checks must pass, and missing checks are silently dropped.** The task score is a strict AND over the verifier results.

`benchmark/executor.py:428-450 @ 271f2c3`
```python
            if verifier.gym_name:
                # Multi-gym: Find the gym config by name
                gym_config = next(
                    (
                        g
                        for g in self.gym_configs
                        if g["mcp_server_name"] == verifier.gym_name
                    ),
                    None,
                )
                if gym_config:
                    database_id = gym_config.get("database_id")
                    context = gym_config.get("context", {})
                    # logger.info(f"  → Using gym '{verifier.gym_name}' database: {database_id}")
                else:
                    logger.warning(
                        f"  ⚠️ Gym '{verifier.gym_name}' not found in gym_servers_config!"
                    )
                    # verification_results[verifier_name] = {
                    #     "passed": False,
                    #     "error": f"Gym '{verifier.gym_name}' not found in configuration",
                    # }
                    continue
```

A verifier that names an unknown domain server is skipped with a warning; the code that would have marked it failed is commented out. Combined with `overall_success = all(v["passed"] for v in verification_results.values())` a few lines later, a task whose verifiers all point at a mis-named server has zero results, and `all([])` is `True`, so it would count as a success. For the released configs this presumably never triggers, but anyone extending the benchmark with new tasks should restore the failing branch.

**6. Scoring script versus README.** `compute_score.py` walks every result JSON in a mode folder (all run folders together, which is how the average over three runs happens), and averages `overall_success_rate`. The README says errored files are "excluded from averages", but the script appends every file's rate to the average and only counts errors separately. An API failure that ends a run early therefore counts as a task failure, not as a missing data point.

**What is missing from the code.** The two most interesting experiments in the paper are the human-plan and Claude-plan conditions. The repo has the `planner_react` orchestrator (an LLM writes a plan that is pasted into the user message under "# Strategic Plan (from Meta Agent)") and the `decomposing` orchestrator, but no orchestrator that feeds the human-written plan, and the task configs have no human-plan field. So the headline "planning is the bottleneck" result cannot be reproduced from the public release as it stands.

**Numbers in the README differ from the paper.** The README's leaderboard shows Claude Opus 4.5 at 39.4 and Sonnet 4.5 at 34.1, and the intro says "Best model achieves only **34.1%** success rate". The per-domain numbers are identical to Table 2. The README average is the simple mean of the eight domain columns (Opus: 315.4 / 8 = 39.4), while the paper's 37.4 is computed another way the paper does not state (possibly weighted by task count). The "34.1%" headline is Sonnet 4.5's README average, which is stale since the README table itself lists better models, including newer Claude Opus 4.6 at 45.9.

## Limitations worth keeping in mind

The oracle-tool setting is generous: the agent sees only about a dozen tools per task, chosen from the gold path. That is fine for isolating planning, but it also leaks a hint about which steps are needed; the presence of `update_hr_case` in the tool list is itself called "a planning signal" in Appendix C.

Refusal is measured on only 30 tasks, so each task is worth over 3 points and differences like 53.9 vs 53.8 are noise.

The adversarial filtering against GPT-5, Gemini and Claude during construction means scores are lower by design and the cross-model comparison may be biased toward models that were not in the filter (the open models were not).

The whole setting is single-turn with no user to ask. The policy prompts often say "Do not ask for any information or confirmation from the user". Real enterprise agents can ask for clarification; here, ambiguity must be resolved alone, which inflates the planning burden relative to deployment. Contrast τ²-bench, which simulates a user.

The strict all-checks-pass rule with fixed IDs means one omitted field fails the task (the CSM case above passed 4 of 5 checks). This is honest for production, where a missed state transition is a real bug, but it makes pass@1 a harsh metric; the verifier-level numbers in Table 6 (around 50–65%) tell the gentler half of the story.

## Why this matters

For anyone building RL environments for agents, this is a worked example of the pattern "tools are database writes, reward is a SQL query on the final state", done at a scale (164 tables, 512 tools, 1,150 tasks) that is hard to reach by hand. The per-run fresh database, the unique-final-state rule, and the three-way split of checks into completion, integrity and compliance are directly reusable design choices. The finding that a 4B model with a good plan beats a frontier model without one suggests where training signal is most needed: in plan generation under constraints, not in tool calling. It also fits the broader picture in [[enterprise-agent-evaluation-challenges]] and ServiceNow's related [[2510.01353 - MemTrack Multi-Platform Agent Memory Benchmark]], where cross-system state is the recurring hard part. A natural next step would be to reward intermediate progress ([[progress-rate-evaluation-for-intermediate-task-states]]) using the verifier-level checks, which the benchmark already has.

## Key claims

1. **The best model completes only about a third of tasks.** Claude Opus 4.5 averages 37.4% pass@1, and open-source models trail. Setup: ReAct loop, oracle tools, 1,150 tasks, average over three runs.
> The best overall model, Claude Opus 4.5, achieves only 37.4%, with open-source models lagging further behind.
(Section 1, Introduction)

2. **Policy-light domains are much easier than policy-heavy ones.** Around 51–52% on Email, Teams, Drive versus 28.5% on ITSM and 30.7% on Hybrid. Setup: best model per domain, Table 2.
> Models fare best on collaboration tasks, with top models reaching 51–52% on Email, Teams, and Drive, but drop sharply on policy-governed domains such as ITSM (28.5%) and cross-domain Hybrid tasks (30.7%).
(Section 1, Introduction)

3. **Human plans lift performance by 14–35 points, far more than LLM plans or extra architecture.** Setup: executors Kimi-K2, Qwen3-30B, Qwen3-4B on CSM, ITSM, HR; Claude Sonnet 4.5 as the automated planner (Table 3).
> Our plan-conditioned ablations demonstrate that humanauthored plans yield 14–35 percentage point gains across models and domains which is far larger than gains from automated planning or more complex multi-agent orchestration.
(Section 5, Discussion)

4. **A small model with a good plan can match or beat much bigger ones.** Qwen3-4B on CSM rises from 3.8% to 37.2% with human plans (Table 3 arithmetic), above Opus 4.5's unaided 34.2%.
> Notably, Qwen3-4B with human-authored plans (and Claude plans) is competitive with or outperforms larger models under the same condition.
(Section 4.4)

5. **Distractor tools do not hurt.** +0.07, +2.35, +0.64 points for 5, 10, 15 extra tools. Setup: Claude Sonnet 4.5, distractors picked by Claude as the most relevant-looking.
> Surprisingly, performance remained remarkably stable. The average completion rates actually increased slightly by an average of ∼1.0% (+0.07% for +5, +2.35% for +10, and +0.64% for +15 tools).
(Section 4.3)

6. **Splitting a task among sub-agents can make things worse.** Planner+Decompose+Subtask falls below plain ReAct on CSM, 16.2% vs 16.7%. Setup: Claude Sonnet 4.5, CSM/ITSM/HR (Figure 6).
> While it provides a minor lift in ITSM, it regresses in both CSM and HR, even falling below the base ReAct performance in CSM (16.2% vs. 16.7%).
(Section 4.4)

7. **Refusal of impossible or forbidden tasks is about a coin flip.** Best clean-refusal rate 53.9%. Setup: 30 infeasible tasks, about 10 checks each, success means no side effects.
> As seen in Table 2, GPT-5.2 (Low) and DeepSeek-V3.2 (High) perform the best (53.9% and 53.8% respectively) in abstaining from the task while leaving no side effects on the system,
(Section 4.3)

8. **Success decays with task length.** Closed-model mean falls from about 35% at 4 steps to under 20% at 16. Setup: tasks grouped by gold-trajectory length (Figure 4).
> The closed-source group, led by Claude Opus 4.5, demonstrates greater resilience, maintaining a performance lead even as the group mean drops from approximately 35% at 4 steps to under 20% by step 16.
(Section 4.3)

9. **Policy compliance is the weakest verifier category.** For example 30.0% in ITSM and 45.5% in CSM, against higher integrity and completion rates (Table 7).
> Models achieve highest scores on Integrity Constraints (system state validity), followed by Task Completion, with Policy Compliance showing the lowest performance.
(Appendix D, Table 7 caption)

10. **Low reasoning effort nearly zeroes out policy-heavy domains.** GPT-OSS-120B at low effort: CSM 1.1%, ITSM 1.1%, HR 0.0%; high effort lifts Drive from 8.6% to 41.0% but ITSM plateaus at 6.1% (Figure 5).
> Operating at a low thinking budget causes the model to struggle severely, achieving nearzero accuracy on complex service and people-facing domains such as CSM (1.1%), ITSM (1.1%), and HR (0.0%).
(Section 4.3)

11. **Gemini-3-Flash is the best value among closed models.** 31.9% at $0.03 per task versus GPT-5 at 29.8% for $0.16 and Sonnet 4.5 at 30.9% for $0.26 (Figure 1).
> It achieves 31.9% performance at 0.03 USD per task, delivering a higher success rate than more expensive models like GPT-5 (29.8% at 0.16 USD) and Claude Sonnet 4.5 (30.9% at 0.26 USD) at a fraction of the cost (80–90% less).
(Section 4.3)

12. **Each run gets a fresh database, so runs are isolated and reproducible.** Confirmed in code: `create_database_from_file` per gym per run, deleted afterwards (`benchmark/executor.py:323-349`, `553-563`).
> To ensure reproducibility and isolation, a fresh database instance is initialized for each task run, preventing state leakage or side effects from prior executions.
(Appendix A.4)
